beats.narration_text: Salaam — Liam, in for Bear. Final episode, 6 of 6. Everything is built, audited, broken, and gated. What is left is the part deployers actually consume: how the tool talks about its own ignorance, the five-to-eight minute video that argues your case to a non-specialist, the disclosure with the one field no AI can write for you, the frictional reflection that closes the loop you opened in episode 1 — and the ship checklist, because this assignment has five automatic deductions and every one of them is avoidable. Uncertainty communication is woven through the grading of components 1 and 4 and the video's clarity — five points on paper, but it decides how everything else reads. Let's land it.

beats.narration_text: Uncertainty communication has three required artifacts, and they share one standard: no overstating, no understating. First, a visualization that includes the uncertainty — the recommendation with its interval drawn on, not a bar chart of point estimates with the doubt exiled to a footnote. If the interval on 'move forty units to warehouse B' includes 'move nothing,' the viewer should see that with their own eyes. Second, a plain sentence a non-specialist would trust. Not 'the model achieves an R-squared of point seven three.' More like: 'the tool is usually right about which site needs more stock, but the amount it suggests is a rough estimate — treat the number as a starting point, not an order.' Notice that sentence gives away real ground. That is what makes it trustworthy. Third, the explicit boundary: here is where I would NOT trust this tool. New sites with under a quarter of history. Weeks containing a holiday. Any unit whose demand pattern changed since the training window. Write the boundary like you will be held to it — because a deployer will hold you to it. Then the video: five to eight minutes, for a non-specialist, and the assignment names its three beats — what it reallocates, the most surprising failure you found, and what a deployer needs to know that the accuracy number alone would not tell them. Lead with the failure. It is the most valuable thing you built, and it is the one thing no other submission will have.

lines: Three artifacts, one standard: no overstating, no understating
A viz with the doubt IN it
A plain sentence a non-specialist would trust

beats.narration_text: Two required gates, both ungraded for points and both minus ten if missing or faked. First, close the frictional loop. In episode 1 you predicted: the hardest failure, the causal validity, your confidence as a number. Now, immediately after finishing, write the reflection: what actually happened, where the prediction was wrong, and what that says about your calibration. Be specific about the miss. 'I predicted the join would be the failure at seventy percent confidence; the join was fine — the failure was seasonality I did not even list. My seventy percent was confidence in the wrong hypothesis.' That sentence is the course working as designed: it is how you find out whether you are getting better at knowing what you know. Second, the AI Use Disclosure — five fields, and the last one is the assignment in miniature: What the AI could not do. The rubric shows you exactly what passes: 'the model recommended reallocating budget toward the channel with the highest observed ROI, but that ROI was confounded by seasonality it had no way to see — I know Q4 spend always over-performs because I ran last year's campaign. The correlation it optimized would not survive the intervention.' Study why that works: a concrete instance, from your build, where your domain knowledge, your values, or your accountability did something the model structurally could not. 'AI can't understand context' is a category claim, and category claims are an automatic minus ten. If you did the work of episodes 2 through 5, you have already met your specific instance. It is probably the moment you overrode the tool. Write that moment down.

lines: Reflection + disclosure — ungraded, and −10 each if missing
Reflection: what happened , where the prediction missed , what it
'My 70% was confidence in the wrong hypothesis'

beats.narration_text: The ship checklist. Four submission items on Canvas by the deadline: the GitHub repo link — runnable tool plus validation report, with a README that explains how to run it; the video, five to eight minutes, unlisted link or file; the frictional journal, prediction timestamped before and reflection after; and the disclosure block on the report. File naming: last name, first name, ReallocationEngine, PDF or Markdown. Repo and video links go in the Canvas submission comment. Now the deduction table, because it is a map of every way to lose points you already earned. Missing journal: minus ten. Category-only disclosure: minus ten. Missing video: minus ten. Tool doesn't run from the repo: minus fifteen — so clone your own repo fresh, on a machine that isn't yours if you can, and follow your own README verbatim. Engine moves a real resource with no hard stop and no justification: minus fifteen. Correlation asserted as cause with zero interrogation: minus ten. That is seventy points of pure process discipline. And one more ceiling to aim past: eighty points is reachable on the core rubric alone — the last twenty are norm-referenced against your cohort, and the rubric tells you what wins them: the skeptical check nobody else thought to run, the causal honesty nobody else had the nerve to state, the hard-stop design that would actually survive deployment. Everyone will have a tool that runs. Not everyone will have a tool that doubts. Ship the doubting one.

lines: Four items , six deductions , one ceiling worth aiming past
Naming: LastName_FirstName_ReallocationEngine.[pdf|md] — links in the Canvas comment.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Say What It Cannot Know and Ship — and for the series. The engine's last mile is linguistic: a visualization with the doubt drawn in, a plain sentence that earns trust by giving ground, and a written boundary where you yourself would not trust the tool. The video leads with the most surprising failure, because the failure is the contribution. The reflection closes the calibration loop you opened before building, and the disclosure names the concrete moment your knowledge did what the model structurally could not — usually the moment you overrode it. Then process discipline: seventy points of deductions exist purely to punish sloppy shipping, so run the checklist like a preflight. The series in one sentence: a reallocation engine is dangerous because it fails invisibly while acting on the world — so you gated its data, audited who it starves, caught its explanation lying, priced its causal claims honestly, found where it flips, and chained its hands before it moves anything real. That is what a useful tool that doubts itself looks like. Ship it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — the last one, and it has a twist. The prompt to paste into Claude reads: Here is my full validation report draft: paste it. Act as the grader for INFO 7375. Find the load-bearing claim you are most confident is wrong or overstated — the one that, if it fails, takes the most of my argument down with it — and say why. Then list what a deployer would need to know that my accuracy and uncertainty numbers do not tell them. Do not be polite. Why this prompt: the assignment's own resource list says it — use the AI to draft, then find the load-bearing thing it got confidently wrong. Running the grader pass inverts it: now the AI hunts for the load-bearing thing YOU got confidently wrong, which is the cheapest red team you will ever hire. But here is the twist to sit with: there is one deliverable this prompt cannot touch. Claude can critique your report, draft your gate, rank your confounders — but the field 'What the AI could not do' is structurally unwritable by the AI, because the moment it writes something there, that something is a thing the AI could do. That field is a small proof that the irreducibly human part of this course is not a slogan. You finish it alone, with your name on it. Thanks for building along — the whole series is on the channel. Liam, in for Bear.
